Thus, ‘the matter is very near to you’ refers to the healing of repentance, achieved when it is ‘in your mouth and in your heart, to perform it.’ Alternatively, with the help of Heaven, when the Hebrew words peh, ‘mouth,’ and lev, ‘heart,’ are spelled out in full as peh-heh, heh-yod, lamed-mem-dalet, bet-yod-tav, their numerical value is tokef, ‘strength,’ alluding to the strength a person gains when mouth and heart are joined. This number also equals kedushah elyonah, ‘supernal holiness,’ for through the combined perfection of mouth and heart a person merits supernal holiness. Peh and lev when spelled out also equal shofar, alluding to the fact that the awakening to repentance symbolized by the shofar—as our Sages said, ‘Shofar: improve, shapperu, your deeds’—must be complete in mouth and heart together, not in the mouth alone. It is known that every aspect of the shofar alludes to repentance. Our Sages therefore said that the Mitzvah is performed with a ram's horn, which was explained as alluding to the need to repent while one's physical vigor remains strong; shofar therefore has the numerical value of tokef, ‘strength.’ The shofar must also be bent, alluding to a penitent whose heart is bowed and humbled, as the gaon Shelah, of blessed memory, explained at length in his allusions of the shofar to repentance. The initial sequence tekiah, shevarim, teruah, tekiah has the following meaning. Tekiah alludes to joy and goodness, while shevarim and teruah allude to distress and suffering: one is a wailing sound and the other a groaning sound. Therefore, as Levush, of blessed memory, states, tekiah and shevarim are not sounded in one continuous duration and one breath, because one alludes to joy and the other to its opposite, and they should not be mixed. The well-known story tells of a man who made a ring and inscribed upon it, ‘This too shall pass.’ When distressed, he would look at it and be comforted; when prospering, he would look at it and not become proud of his prosperity and wealth, because he would reflect that this too would pass and had no permanence. Similarly, after tekiah, which alludes to goodness and joy, we sound shevarim, which alludes to distress and suffering, teaching a person not to become proud of his prosperity or haughty of heart, for he must remember that sorrow may follow joy. After teruah, which alludes to distress and suffering, we again sound tekiah, which alludes to goodness, teaching one who suffers not to despair of mercy but to reflect that honor will ultimately come and he will see days of goodness and joy. The tekiah, alluding to goodness, is one long, continuous sound, teaching that goodness will come all at once, without stages. Shevarim consists of short sounds, teaching that suffering comes little by little. Thus the Sages explained the verse ‘HaShem will be a stronghold for the oppressed, a stronghold in times of distress’ (Psalms 9:10): He divides one great period of distress into small periods so that a person can endure them and not die. The shape of the shofar, which symbolizes awakening to repentance, has one wide end and one narrow end, and one must blow through the narrow end. The portion held in the hand thus continually widens, alluding to the fact that a penitent must continually increase in the service of HaShem, as our Sages said: ‘The older Torah scholars become, the more wisdom is added to them’ (Shabbat 152a). Its shape, with one narrow and one wide end, and the requirement to blow through the narrow end, also alludes to the letter heh of repentance, which has two openings, one wide and one narrow. The penitent should enter through the narrow opening, for in this way the matter receives assistance, as stated in the Gemara. Alternatively, its shape alludes to the narrow end below and the wide end above. In lower matters connected to the pleasures of this world, the penitent should restrict and limit himself; in matters above, matters of the soul, he should act expansively and abundantly. Alternatively, it appears to me, with the help of Heaven, that the shofar's shape may be understood through the episode concerning Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya in Eruvin 53b. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya said: ‘No person ever defeated me except a woman, a boy, and a girl. What happened with the woman? Once I lodged at an inn. On the first day the hostess made me beans; I ate them and left nothing. On the second day I likewise left nothing. On the third day she oversalted them. When I tasted them, I withdrew my hand. She asked, “Rabbi, why are you not eating?” I replied, “I already ate earlier today.” She said, “Then you should have withdrawn your hand from the bread.” She further said, “Rabbi, perhaps you did not leave pe'ah from the earlier portions. Did the Sages not say that one does not leave pe'ah in the cooking pot, but one leaves pe'ah in the serving dish?” What happened with the girl? Once I was walking on a road that passed through a field, and I walked upon it. A girl said to me, “Rabbi, is this not a field?” I replied, “Is it not a well-trodden road?” She said, “Robbers like you trod it down.” What happened with the boy? Once I was traveling and saw a boy sitting at a crossroads. I asked him, “Which road should we take to the city?” He replied, “This one is short and long, and that one is long and short.” I took the short and long road. When I reached the city, I found gardens and orchards surrounding it. I turned back and said, “My son, did you not tell me it was short?” He replied, “And did I not tell you it was long?” I kissed him on the head and said, “Fortunate are you, Israel, for you are all great Sages, from your greatest to your smallest.”’ These conclude the words of the Gemara. The gaon Chida, of blessed memory, explained in Petach Einayim that these incidents did not literally occur. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya related them as parables in order to teach moral correction. It is known that human life is divided into three periods: days of ascent, days of stability, and days of decline. During the first two periods, ascent and stability, a person follows the materiality of this world, satisfies his desires with its vanities and pleasures, and does not turn to the concerns of the World to Come. Only during the days of decline, when his strength weakens, does he separate himself and begin a path of repentance. This is the meaning of ‘I lodged at an inn’: the inn is this world. ‘She made me beans,’ polin, whose letters allude to peloni, ‘the unnamed one,’ meaning that this world invited him to the desires of coarse matter that derive from ‘the unnamed one.’ On the first day, the period of ascent, he consumed the pleasures and enjoyments of this world and left none of his time for the World to Come. On the second day, the period of stability, he did likewise. On the third day, the period of decline, ‘she oversalted them’: he no longer retained strength for the pleasures of this world, and pains surrounded his body and the powers of his limbs on every side. When he came to taste, he was compelled to withdraw from pleasures and began to repent. The soul then came to arouse him more strongly to repentance, having found an opportunity to speak words that would enter his heart. To begin the conversation and arouse him to repentance, she first asked, ‘Why do you not dine today upon the pleasures of this world as you did in the earlier periods?’ He replied, ‘I already dined in those periods, when my belly became filled with harmful things; how long can this continue?’ The soul said, ‘You should have withdrawn your hand from the bread.’ That is, if you remember your earlier deeds and regret them, it is not enough merely to withdraw from pleasures. You need afflictions and fasts, withdrawing your hand even from bread, which is greatly necessary for maintaining the body. She further asked, ‘Perhaps you left nothing for the World to Come during the days that passed. Did the Sages not say: One does not leave pe'ah in the ilpas, the cooking pot?’ This alludes to the time specifically designated for Torah study: ilpas can be read alef-samekh, meaning the study of sixty tractates. From that time one should leave no edge for worldly matters. ‘But one leaves pe'ah in the ke'arah, the serving dish’: from the time designated for worldly affairs, which resembles a serving dish and is temporary life—chayei sha'ah having the same numerical value as ke'arah—one leaves a portion for the World to Come, seizing some of this time and sanctifying it with the holiness of Torah. How, then, did you waste all your earlier days entirely upon the vanities of this world? The incident involving the girl conveys moral correction to the people of the age who act against Torah law. If a Sage tells them that a practice is forbidden, they answer, ‘Such is the custom of the world.’ It is proper to reply, ‘Robbers like you trod down this road.’ Those who adopted such a practice robbed the Holy One, blessed be He, by violating the law. Through it, the kelippah draws nourishment from holy bounty, and there is no greater theft than this. The boy in the story alludes to the good inclination, which is called ‘a poor and wise child’ (Ecclesiastes 4:13). Rabbi Yehoshua asked him, ‘Which road should we take to the city of G-d?’—the Garden of Eden. He replied, ‘This one is short and long,’ meaning the road of the wicked. The evil inclination makes it appear short in this world, without the labor of serving HaShem, but from the perspective of the World to Come it is long. Upon death, a wicked person does not immediately receive his proper place in the Garden of Eden; he must return through many reincarnations and be judged in Gehinnom for many years until he is fit to reach his place there. The road of the righteous, who engage and labor in Torah, Mitzvot, and good deeds in this world, is long and short: in this world it is long, involving great effort and toil for the body, but from the perspective of the World to Come it is short, for immediately after departing this world the righteous person goes to the city of G-d, to be illuminated by the light of life. This is the substance of his explanation; see there. Thus the sinner walks a short and long road, following the material pleasure visible to his eyes without considering the ultimate outcome. The shofar comes to awaken sinners to repentance, so the blower must blow through the narrow end, causing the sound to travel first through the narrow part and then through the wide part, because it comes to awaken the hearts of sinners who walk the short and long road. The righteous, who walk the long and short road, do not need the shofar to awaken them. We find in the laws of the shofar that it is valid only when it is naturally a hollow tube containing a solid core from its original formation. If one removed the core and hollowed it out by human action to make a tube, it is invalid. This alludes to the parable in the boy's story. People perform acts forbidden by Torah law and claim that they constitute custom. If a custom is permitted according to the Torah of HaShem, it is a good custom and must be upheld, for that road was opened by Heaven. If the custom contradicts the Torah of HaShem and the road was opened only by people who permitted the matter to themselves, the Hebrew word minhag, ‘custom,’ contains the same letters as Gehinnom, and it is forbidden to follow that road. Likewise, shofar denotes a tube. It is fit to convey the sound only when the tube was opened by Heaven; if a person made the tube himself by hollowing out the core and turning it into a shofar, it is invalid. Our Sages said that the minimum measure of a shofar is enough for one to grasp it in his hand while some remains visible on either side (Rosh Hashanah 27b). This alludes to the moral teaching in the foregoing episode of the woman. The soul rebuked the person for wasting all his time upon the vanities of this world and leaving no portion during his days of ascent and stability for the World to Come. A person certainly cannot engage in Torah all day and all night, for many followed the path of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and did not succeed (Berakhot 35b); he must engage in worldly affairs. Nevertheless, he must set fixed times for Torah and time for worldly business. In this way he will always grasp the path of repentance in his hand throughout his days, with the shofar visible ‘on either side’: he will consider which hours of the day to devote to worldly business in order to provide food for his household and which hours of day and night to devote to Torah. He will keep the path of repentance in his hand and never loosen his hold upon it. This is the allusion in the measure of the shofar, which symbolizes repentance: he grasps it in his hand, and it is visible on either side. Alternatively, it appears to me, with the help of Heaven, that this law concerning the shofar's measure alludes to the need for moderation even in repentance. This is a great principle in both physical and bodily matters and spiritual matters of the soul. Ben HaMelekh VeHaNazir relates that a king stood before his teacher at the teacher's death and said, ‘I am ready; instruct me.’ The teacher replied, ‘Take care that you not be moist and become squeezed dry, not dry and break, not sweet and be sucked dry, and not bitter and become despised.’ See there. I explained that he divided his teaching into two parts. The first concerns matters of the soul: ‘Do not be moist and become squeezed dry.’ If a person seeks to repent by multiplying fasts and afflictions beyond what his constitution can bear, this will certainly empty all strength from his body until he dies, and HaShem does not desire this. Thus he said: Do not be so moist that the fasts and afflictions squeeze all the strength and moisture from your body, leaving it empty until you die. ‘Nor dry and break’ means: do not harden your heart like dry wood, refusing to submit and repent, for then your sins will break you, as it is written, ‘One who hardens his heart will fall into evil’ (Proverbs 28:14). The second part concerns bodily and material matters: do not be so sweet that you multiply gifts and benefit people excessively, for then people will swarm upon you, consume your money, and leave you empty; HaShem does not desire this. Nor be so bitter that you become extremely miserly and stingy, for then you will be despised in heaven and on earth. Since a person must follow moderation even on the path of repentance, the Sages said that the shofar symbolizing repentance must be held with a moderate grasp, so that it remains visible on either side. Alternatively, it appears to me, with the help of Heaven, that ‘he grasps it in his hand and it is visible on either side’ means the following. The Hebrew letters immediately preceding the letters of shofar form akarah, ‘barren,’ while the letters immediately following shofar have the numerical value 797, equal to sekharkha harbeh me'od, ‘your reward is exceedingly great.’ This alludes to the fact that before repentance, the sinner's soul was barren, without children—meaning Mitzvot and good deeds—as explained concerning the verse ‘These are the offspring of Noah—Noah.’ After he repented and his deliberate sins were transformed into merits, he was told, ‘Your reward is exceedingly great,’ for he has immense reward, and complete righteous people cannot stand in the place where penitents stand. Thus, ‘he grasps the shofar in his hand and it is visible on either side’ means that he should examine the letters before shofar and the letters after shofar and learn great moral instruction from them. The letters before shofar also have the numerical value 375, equal to kelal uferat, ‘general and particular.’ This alludes to the fact that a penitent must consider in his repentance both the particular sins he committed himself and what occurred within Israel as a whole, for all Israel are responsible for one another. The letters after shofar have the numerical value 797, also equal to yishuv hada'at, ‘settled consciousness.’ This alludes to rectification for the sin of wasting seed, which is a rectification of da'at, since erection occurs only through da'at. Our Sages therefore said that the son of David will come only when attention is diverted. Alternatively, with the help of Heaven, ‘it is visible on either side’ may be understood according to what our master Rabbi Moshe Alshekh, of blessed memory, wrote in this parashah. A pious person would honor everyone. Concerning one older than himself, he would say, ‘This person has performed more Mitzvot than I.’ Concerning one greater in wisdom, he would say, ‘I am certainly obligated to honor him.’ Concerning one younger than himself, he would say, ‘He has not committed as many sins as I.’ Concerning one less wise than himself, he would say, ‘He will not be held as accountable for his sins as I, since in comparison with me he is judged as having acted unwittingly.’ See there. This counsel also helps a person become jealous of others' Mitzvot while regarding himself as lower than everyone. Thus, ‘it is visible on either side’: he looks both toward those older than he and those younger. It also appears to me that ‘visible on either side’ refers to sins between a person and the Omnipresent and sins between one person and another. It further appears to me, with the help of Heaven, to follow the teaching, ‘Know from where you came and where you are going’ (Avot 3:1). Through these two perspectives a person acquires submission and humility, and acceptance of repentance depends upon humility of heart, as it is written, ‘The sacrifices of G-d are a broken spirit’ and ‘A broken and contrite heart, G-d, You will not despise’ (Psalms 51:19). Therefore, the Sages instituted fasting on the eve of Rosh Hashanah so that a person enters the Ten Days of Repentance with submission and a broken heart, for fasting produces humility in the heart. Most of the community has adopted this fast on the eve of Rosh Hashanah, and it is not considered ostentation if others know that one is fasting. This fast has support in Midrash Tanchuma, as explained by Levush, of blessed memory. It is therefore good for every person to observe it, except one who is very weak, an elderly person, or a child.

essence.en: Ben Ish Chai presents eating on the eve of Yom Kippur as a Mitzvah and joins that preparation with the intention to act for the sake of Heaven. Readiness for the holy day includes the ordinary act of a meal. The passage directs that act toward its sacred purpose, asking that bodily preparation and inward intention accompany one another.
essence.he: הבן איש חי מציג את האכילה בערב יום הכיפורים כמצווה ומצרף להכנה זו כוונה לעשות לשם שמים. המוכנות ליום הקדוש כוללת גם את המעשה הרגיל של סעודה. הקטע מכוון אותו אל תכליתו שבקדושה ומבקש שההכנה הגופנית והכוונה הפנימית ילוו זו את זו.

source.he: אמרו חכמינו זכרונם לברכה: "מצוה לאכול בערב יום הכפורים ולהרבות בסעודה", וכתבו המקובלים ז"ל שצריך לאכול שיעור שני ימים, אם יוכל האדם לאכול כ"ל כך, כדי לתקן יום זה באכילה מה שצריך ליום זה ומה שצריך ליום מחר שהוא יום הכפורים הקדוש, והאדם יעשה כל מעשיו לשם שמים והשם יתברך לא ימנע טוב להולכים בתמים, וכתבו האחרונים ז"ל שמצוה לאכול דגים בערב יום הכפורים בשחרית דוקא, ויש לזה קצת סמך מן המדרש ועיין ב"מטה אפרים", ונראה שיש טעם לזה כי הדגים רומזים לעינא פקיחא המאירה ביסוד שהוא בחינת היום הזה בסוד הפסוק "בן פרת יוסף בן פרת עלי עין" (בראשית מט כב), וטוב עין הוא יבורך:
source.en: Our Sages, of blessed memory, said: ‘It is a Mitzvah to eat on the eve of Yom Kippur and to increase the meal.’ The Kabbalists, of blessed memory, wrote that if a person is able, he should eat the amount of food needed for two days, in order to rectify through eating both what this day requires and what the following holy day of Yom Kippur requires. A person should perform all his deeds for the sake of Heaven, and HaShem, blessed be He, will withhold no good from those who walk with integrity. The later authorities, of blessed memory, wrote that it is a Mitzvah to eat fish specifically in the morning on the eve of Yom Kippur. There is some support for this in the Midrash; see Mateh Ephraim. It appears that the reason is that fish allude to the ever-watchful eye that illuminates Yesod, which is the aspect of this day, in the secret of the verse ‘A fruitful son is Joseph, a fruitful son by a spring’ (Genesis 49:22). ‘One with a good eye will be blessed.’

essence.en: Ben Ish Chai distinguishes dwelling in the sukkah’s open space beneath its covering from sleeping beneath a sufficiently high bed or table inside it. Entering the structure is not the entire question; where one actually rests also matters. His teaching turns attention to the concrete form in which the Mitzvah is being lived.
essence.he: הבן איש חי מבחין בין הישיבה באוויר הסוכה תחת סככה לבין שינה תחת מיטה או שולחן גבוהים בתוכה. הכניסה למבנה אינה כל הבירור; חשוב גם המקום שבו האדם נח בפועל. דבריו מפנים את הקשב לצורה הממשית שבה המצווה מתקיימת.

source.he: צריך לישב באויר סוכה, והישן תחת המטה אם יש מגג המטה עד לארץ עשרה טפחים לא יצא ידי חובתו, וצריך ליזהר שלא ישן תחת שלחן שגבוה עשרה טפחים:
source.en: One must sit beneath the open air of the sukkah. One who sleeps beneath a bed does not fulfill his obligation if there are ten handbreadths from the top of the bed to the ground. One must also take care not to sleep beneath a table ten handbreadths high.

title.en: Let the season end in renewed prayer

essence.en: In the Vezot Haberakhah section, Ben Ish Chai describes Hoshana Rabbah as the conclusion of the days of repentance beginning in Elul. He calls for increased prayer and supplication at this completion. The closing of the season becomes an invitation to renewed appeal, giving its final days the seriousness of a spiritual conclusion.
essence.he: בפרק וזאת הברכה מתאר הבן איש חי את הושענא רבה כחתימת ימי התשובה שמתחילים באלול. הוא קורא להרבות בתפילה ובתחנונים בשעת סיום זו. חתימת הזמן נעשית הזמנה לבקשה מחודשת ומעניקה לימיו האחרונים את כובדה של חתימה רוחנית.

source.he: מרבים בתפילות ותחנונים בהושענא רבה, כי הוא סיום נ"א יום שנתנו לישראל בחסד עליון לעשות בהם תשובה ותתקבל תשובתם, והם שלשים דאלול מיום ראשון של ר"ח וכ"א יום דתשרי רמז לדבר אין נא אלא לשון בקשה לכך נתנו נ"א יום לצורך הבקשות ותחנונים ויום זה הוא סיום יום נ"א, ולכן נקרא הושענ"א רבא כלומר הושע את יום נ"א שהוא רבא דהכל הולך אחר החתום:
source.en: One increases prayers and supplications on Hoshana Rabbah, for it concludes the fifty-one days that were granted to Israel through supernal kindness in which to repent and have their repentance accepted. These are the thirty days of Elul, beginning with the first day of Rosh Chodesh, and twenty-one days of Tishrei. An allusion is found in the teaching that the word na denotes a plea; accordingly, fifty-one—nun-alef—days were granted for pleas and supplications, and this day concludes the fifty-first day. It is therefore called Hoshana Rabbah, meaning: Save the fifty-first day, which is great, for everything follows the conclusion.
